# Jacek Karpiński: Polish Computer Pioneer
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a Polish engineer and computer scientist whose work was instrumental in advancing computing in Poland. After surviving traumatic injuries and resistance activities during World War II, he completed higher education in engineering and began his career with innovative projects such as the Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH, 1957) and the AKAT-1 (1959), the world’s first transistor-based analyzer for differential equations. Karpiński's work earned him an international UNESCO scholarship, allowing him to visit leading U.S. technology centers and meet renowned scientists like Claude Shannon. Returning to Poland, he built one of the world’s first perceptrons (1964) and developed the KAR-65 computer (1968), which was the fastest Polish computer of its time.
Karpiński’s most ambitious project was the K-202 minicomputer, developed in the early 1970s using cutting-edge microchip technology. The K-202 had features that rivaled Western computers, including modularity, advanced memory management, and high-speed performance. Despite technical excellence, the project was hindered by political opposition, lack of support from state computer manufacturers, and administrative challenges, resulting in limited production. Later in life, Karpiński worked abroad and returned to Poland, continuing to pursue technological innovation. He received both the Officer's and Commander's Crosses of Polonia Restituta. His legacy is debated, but he is widely recognized for his pioneering role in Polish computing and for his unique contributions, often in the face of considerable adversity.
